Two Tankers Hit Iranian Mines in Strait of Hormuz

Severity: WARNING Detected: 2026-11-25T06:17:58.930Z

Summary

Iranian media report two additional oil tankers struck Iranian naval mines in the southern and eastern Strait of Hormuz while transiting on “unauthorised routes.” This compounds earlier reported incidents and elevates the perceived risk of deliberate mine warfare in the chokepoint, implying a higher risk premium for seaborne crude and product flows through the Gulf.

Details

The latest reports from Iranian media indicate that two more oil tankers have struck Iranian naval mines in the southern and eastern sections of the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of this morning. The vessels were reportedly travelling on “unauthorised routes,” which Tehran will frame as a rules-enforcement issue, but market participants will read more broadly as evidence that live mines are now an operational hazard in multiple zones of the strait.
Roughly 17–20 million b/d of crude and condensate, plus large volumes of refined products and NGLs, transit the Strait of Hormuz. Even without a full closure, credible evidence of active mines in more than one part of the chokepoint forces shipowners, P&I clubs, and charterers to reassess routing, speed, and insurance coverage. Immediate physical supply is not yet clearly curtailed, but effective capacity can be impaired if traffic slows, certain lanes are avoided, or more vessels sit idle pending risk assessments or naval escort.
The primary impact is a higher geopolitical and maritime-risk premium on Gulf-linked benchmarks.

...

Fuel oil and middle distillate markets in Asia could see added tightness if traffic congestion or rerouting emerges.
Historical analogues include the 2019 tanker incidents and the 1980s “Tanker War,” both of which generated several-dollar risk premia in Brent despite limited physical loss. If further incidents occur or if Western or GCC navies formally declare mine-clearance operations, the risk premium could expand and persist for weeks to months. If today’s reports remain isolated and are followed by visible de-escalation and safe-passage assurances, the price impact may be partly retraced, but the market will likely retain a structural risk discount on Hormuz transits for some time.

Supertankers burning in Hormuz : are Iranian sea mines real?

By maritimescrimes
November 24, 2026
3 mins read
Footage of the supertanker struck "Tara Gas" the 17 of November in Hormuz. Sources: local social media user on Facebook.
Footage of the supertanker “Tara Gas” struck the 17 of November in Hormuz. Sources: local social media user on Facebook.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards declared two supertankers carrying more than four million barrels had hit mines. The UKMTO and JMIC records for the same week list unknown projectiles, and in fact no sea mine strike has been confirmed.
On Thursday morning the IRGC Navy announced that two supertankers carrying more than four million barrels had struck mines on an ‘unauthorised route’ and were still burning off the southern coast of the strait, Al-Monitor reports . The IRGC gave no ship name, flag or owner, and Al-Monitor could not verify the claim. The New Region reported that the Iranian army added a third tanker hours later, east of the ‘restricted zone’, and said its navigation systems had been switched off.
IRGC declaration on the supertanker struck by the mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Nov. 19. IRNA News Agency. IRGC declaration on the supertanker struck by the mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Nov. 19. IRNA News Agency.

Inconsistence : two versions of the same week

The JMIC log, reported by Gulf News , lists ‘unknown projectiles’ for the strikes that Tehran attributes to naval mines, while the CENTCOM declared that the route has been cleared by the US force and remain so.
Between 13 and 18 November, UKMTO and the JMIC recorded attacks on four tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz: the Tara Gas, the Navig8 Messi, the Dar Salwa and one unnamed vessel. Each is logged as struck by an unknown projectile, and none as struck by a mine. Tehran has claimed mine strikes on four tankers on 16 November, three on 17 November, three on 18 November and two on 19 November, without naming any of them. The only confirmed mine attack of this war, according to the Telegraph , involved limpet mines placed on the tanker Louise 1 on 29 October.

Iran narrative framing

The geography of the Strait of Hormuz complicates claims of a widespread minefield. Moored mines, anchored below the surface, and bottom mines, resting on the seabed, have different deployment constraints depending on water depth, currents and seabed conditions. Drifting mines present a separate, less predictable danger. Yet a substantial minefield across active shipping lanes would create a persistent navigational hazard, making continued commercial transits particularly concerning. The absence of independently confirmed mine detections, combined with ongoing vessel movements, makes claims of extensive mining difficult to substantiate.
Beyond the military threat, Iran’s repeated claims of mine strikes, raise questions about the use of information warfare in the Strait of Hormuz. Announcing attacks on unnamed tankers, without verifiable evidence, can amplify uncertainty and fuel fears among shipping operators, insurers and energy markets.
Such statements may serve a psychological warfare objective: portraying the strait as increasingly dangerous and suggesting that Tehran can disrupt global trade even without establishing a minefield. Whether this is a deliberate coordinated information operation remains unproven, but the potential effect is clear: fear of an attack can disrupt commercial shipping even when the threat itself has not been independently confirmed.

International law reminder

Although not factual, Tehran’s account describes mines in an international strait through and the International law leaves little room for that. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees transit passage that cannot be suspended, and in the Corfu Channel case of 1949 the International Court of Justice found that a state cannot close an international strait to neutral shipping. The 1907 Hague Convention prohibits laying contact mines with the sole aim of intercepting commercial shipping and requires every possible precaution for the safety of peaceful shipping. Iran argues that these rules bind only the states that signed them, but the weight of international legal opinion is against that reading.

Clearance capacity

The US retired its last four Bahrain-based minesweepers in September 2025. Its remaining capacity in the Gulf is three littoral combat ships carrying a new clearance package whose effectiveness is unproven. The Telegraph adds that RFA Lyme Bay has been in theater since June with British and French teams and unmanned systems, also new and unproven, and that clearance would have to be carried out within range of Iranian missiles and drones.

Energy transit and conflict resolution path

UKMTO tracking showed single to low double digit daily transits between 15 and 18 November, against about 27 US assisted transits a day and a 2025 baseline of 138, according to Al-Monitor. The Telegraph reports that Abu Dhabi state tankers continue to leave the Gulf, transferring cargo to other ships off Fujairah or Sohar. The JMIC has warned that further attacks are highly likely over the next 24 to 48 hours.
The diplomatic channel could ease the situation ? After the Iron Gate on Iran plan, at Shenzhen, the Trump, Xi and Putin joint statement made no mention of Iran or the Strait of Hormuz. Trump told Xi in their bilateral meeting that both countries have an interest in energy flowing through the strait, Al-Monitor reports. Trump has signalled he will hold off on another major round of strikes until the new year, and Rubio has said economic pressure is achieving the US objective, while US naval deployment remains intense.
Iran’s position is that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has told officials to end the state of ‘neither war nor peace’, and Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf said Hormuz will never return to its pre-war status. Moreover, the escalade might increase collateral damages, Iranian leadership seek to add pressure on USA and its allies, notably mentioning the capability to target US base on the European ground .

Texas Authorizes 10-Block, 2.58-GW Power Plant for AI Campus

State regulators allow a 620-engine generating facility to support Vantage Data Centers' planned $25B data center development near Abilene

By Bryan Gottlieb
Aerial rendering of Vantage's Frontier data center campus with large buildings surrounded by landscaped grounds.
Rendering courtesy Vantage Data Centers
An architectural rendering shows Vantage Data Centers' planned $25B Frontier campus in west Texas, where the state has allowed a nearly 2,6-GW natural gas power plant for the 10-building AI development.
November 25, 2026
Texas regulators have authorized a major expansion of a natural gas-fired power plant designed to supply electricity to a $25-billion artificial intelligence data center development near Abilene.
The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality approved the expansion Nov. 19 , allowing Houston-based VoltaGrid to increase generating capacity at its ABI-1 facility from 709 MW to 2,582 MW.
The permit replaces an earlier authorization for 210 natural gas engines with one covering 620.
The power plant will serve Frontier, Vantage Data Centers' largest campus worldwide, a planned 1,200-acre development in Shackelford County in west Texas.. Spanning nearly two square miles, the $25-billion project will include 10 data centers totaling 3.7 million sq ft and 1.4 GW of critical computing capacity. Part of the Oracle and OpenAI Stargate initiative, Frontier will receive dedicated electricity from a generating facility owned and operated separately by VoltaGrid.

Read More

Voltagrid LLC — Construction Permit, Source Analysis and Technical Review

Under the Nov. 19 authorization, VoltaGrid can construct 10 independently operating power blocks using Jenbacher reciprocating engines. State construction filings identify Kiewit as the design firm for buildings at Frontier, including a 344,796-sq-ft data center with an estimated construction cost of $950 million and a projected completion in August 2027. The filings do not establish Kiewit's role in VoltaGrid's separately owned generating facility.
According to the commission technical review, the configuration includes 250 Jenbacher J620 engines rated at 3.22 MW each and 370 J624 engines rated at 4.80 MW each. VoltaGrid will group the engines in its proprietary QPac modular generating assemblies, each accommodating up to four J620 engines or five J624 engines, along with associated generators and emissions controls. Manufacturer INNIO describes the five-engine J624 configuration as a roughly 25-MW unit designed for rapid deployment and incremental expansion of data center power capacity.
For large modular power installations, the work extends beyond positioning generators on-site. During a Nov. 10 ENR visit to microgrid supplier Mesa Power Solutions ' San Antonio manufacturing facility, CEO Scott Gromer explained that his company's scope typically begins where the natural gas supply reaches its equipment and ends at the electrical switchgear.
"Bring us the gas, take away the electricity for the generation piece," he said.
Gas pipelines, electrical distribution systems and connections to the data center must be coordinated with the generating equipment. At Frontier, contractors responsible for those portions of the work have not been identified. Mesa is not involved in the project.

...

Bottom: A conceptual cutaway illustrates the generator, engine coupling, V-configured cylinders, crankshaft, turbocharging and cooling systems. The rendering is schematic and does not represent a manufacturer-verified internal configuration.
Top: Image courtesy INNIO Bottom: AI-generated illustration by OpenAI for ENR; conceptual rendering.
Supporting infrastructure will include 60 natural gas-fired heaters to condition fuel arriving through a pipeline, 20 diesel-powered black-start engines to restart generating equipment after outages and four bulk urea storage tanks serving the emissions-control systems. Each generating block will also have lubricating-oil storage and associated fuel and electrical equipment.
To control nitrogen oxide emissions, the permit requires selective catalytic reduction systems, along with oxidation catalysts to reduce carbon monoxide and volatile organic compounds. Commission analysis projects potential annual emissions of approximately 10.63 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent under the permitted operating configuration, along with allowable annual emissions of approximately 570 tons of nitrogen oxides and 372 tons of formaldehyde. These figures represent modeled or permitted emissions, not measured pollution from operating equipment.

Permitting Questions and Legal Scrutiny

Approval followed Texas' Nov. 13 resumption of data center permitting after a statewide pause Gov. Greg Abbott imposed in September. The commission had issued a preliminary approval notice for VoltaGrid's ABI-1 facility Sept. 22, one day after the directive, according to regulatory records examined by environmental watchdog groups. Whether the application was subsequently suspended remains unclear.
Under federal Clean Air Act Title V operating-permit requirements administered by the commission, VoltaGrid must submit an initial application before beginning operations, according to the agency's technical review.
Separately, Vantage and VoltaGrid face federal litigation over permitting for gas-fired power facilities serving two data center campuses in San Antonio. The Environmental Integrity Project, Sierra Club and Public Citizen allege the companies proceeded under permits intended for smaller pollution sources rather than obtaining the major-source authorizations required by federal law. The lawsuit does not involve the Frontier development.

...

Climate change and energy

Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom.
By
* Casey Crownhart archive page
November 24, 2026
Gas turbines at the xAI data center in Memphis AP Photo/George Walker IV
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.
xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.
As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.
It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.
Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.
When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.
Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.
“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.
Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.
Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.
The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)
Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.
Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.
BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation.

...

Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.
While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.
“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

Plugging a new data center into the electric grid can mean waiting as long as a decade for approval. In AI, a decade is roughly three eternities.
So a growing number of developers are skipping the line and building their own natural gas power plants on site. The company that made this approach famous, and infamous, is xAI, whose Memphis supercomputer campus has run on dozens of gas turbines since 2024.

How xAI powered Colossus without waiting for the grid

The idea is simple. If the utility can’t deliver enough electricity fast enough, you generate it yourself, right next to the servers.
The industry term is “behind-the-meter” power. Picture a homeowner with a backyard generator, except the generator is a fleet of industrial turbines and the house is a supercomputer.
xAI had its first gas turbines running at the Memphis Colossus site by mid-2024. At the peak, 35 turbines were on site, with roughly 422 MW of nameplate capacity before permanent units replaced them. Some of those early turbines operated without permits.

Regulators eventually caught up with the arrangement. In July 2025, the Memphis site, known as Colossus 1, received a permit for 15 permanent turbines with a combined capacity of approximately 247 megawatts.
The second campus, Colossus 2 in Southaven, Mississippi, operates at a different scale. Regulators approved 41 gas turbines there in March 2026, supplying around 1.2 gigawatts of capacity.

The legal fight that comes with the turbines

In April 2026, the NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against xAI alleging Clean Air Act violations tied to emissions from both the temporary and permanent turbines. The case is still unresolved. In late October 2026, judges denied motions to dismiss, which means the lawsuit continues.
Community concerns center on what gas turbines release into the local air. Running dozens of them near homes is a different proposition than drawing power from a distant plant on the grid.

9 November, 2026 By Audrey Lee

Executive summary

Data centres are increasingly building their own power ‘behind the meter’ (BTM) rather than waiting years for a grid connection. We answer five questions on what that means:
* What is BTM? Power that a data centre produces, stores and uses on its own site. Most sites use it while they wait for a grid connection, but it can stay useful long after the connection arrives.
* How does it vary by region? BTM is largely a US story for now, driven by long grid queues and plentiful gas. Elsewhere, it is smaller and more often powered by renewables.
* Can it compete with the grid on cost? Not on average, but grid constraints, cheap local energy and good financing terms can close much of the gap.
* What else can BTM offer data centres? It can absorb the sudden power swings created by artificial intelligence (AI), cover daily peaks and provide backup, roles that do not end when the grid arrives.
* What does it mean for investors? BTM is more likely to complement the grid than replace it. For grid investors, the bigger risk is speculative demand, although grid operators and regulators are introducing rules to screen it out. We see battery storage as particularly attractive in the value chain, as it remains useful before and after the grid arrives.
BTM may get ahead of the grid, but its long-term value lies alongside it.

What is ‘behind the meter’?

‘Behind the meter’ refers to power generated and stored on the customer’s side of the meter, the point that separates the customer’s own system from the utility’s grid (Figure 1). A household with rooftop solar panels is a small-scale example. At a far larger scale, data centres are increasingly turning to BTM because they cannot afford to wait for the grid. Grid connection queues for data centres have lengthened considerably, a theme we explored in our recent paper, Grid capex in the age of renewables and AI (July 2026). In the main data centre hubs of both the US and Europe, a large new site can now face years of delay while new lines and substations are built. 1
Figure 1. Two sides of the meter: how a data centre can be powered
Source: Macquarie Asset Management analysis.
BTM arrangements take four main forms (Figure 2): 2

Which technologies power BTM at data centres, and how does their use vary by region?

Developers can choose from gas engines, gas turbines, fuel cells, and solar and wind, usually backed by batteries. Small nuclear reactors are a longer-term option (Figure 3). Which they use varies considerably by region. BTM is happening at scale in the US, mostly with gas, because shale gas is plentiful and can supply power around the clock. Outside the US, where gas is more expensive, BTM leans towards renewables, though volumes are still small.
Figure 3. Data centres can draw on a wide range of onsite technologies

* Gas engines | Large versions of a car engine that burn gas to turn a generator. They come in modular units that can be added one at a time. | Main onsite supply, especially where a site grows in stages, and the cheapest onsite gas option. Engines make up about 29% of planned US onsite gas capacity. | Needs a steady gas supply, so a site relying on a single pipeline has no backup if it fails. Running costs track gas prices, which are more than four times higher in Europe than in the US.
* Gas turbines | Burn gas to spin a turbine, much like a jet engine. Some reuse the hot exhaust to make extra power. 3 | Main supply at larger sites. Turbines make up the biggest share of planned US onsite gas capacity, at 55%. | Same gas supply risk as engines, and new machines can take five years or more to arrive.
* Fuel cells | Turn gas into electricity through a chemical reaction rather than burning it, a bit like a battery that is constantly refuelled. | A niche option today, at about 3% of planned US onsite gas capacity, most of it a single project. 4 Lower operational costs than other gas options could give them a bigger role over time. | Same gas supply risk as engines. The lowest operational costs among all gas options, with less local air pollution. But they are also the most expensive to build, so still the costliest overall, though subsidies such as the US investment tax credit can help.

Published Nov 25, 2026 4:57 am ET

(Credit: Saipem)
Saipem has secured two offshore engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) contracts from Aramco in Saudi Arabia worth approximately $650 million, covering production deck manifolds, pipelines, power cables and associated subsea infrastructure.
The awards, designated Contract Release Purchase Orders (CRPOs) 168 and 170, fall under Saipem's existing Long-Term Agreement with Aramco.
The first contract, CRPO 168, covers the EPCI of four production deck manifolds (PDMs), approximately 14 kilometers of pipelines with diameters ranging from 12 to 16 inches, and around 24 kilometers of 15 kV power cables.
The scope also includes associated subsea facilities serving the Abu Safah, Safaniyah, Manifa and Berri fields, alongside onshore tie-in activities at the drill site in the Manifa field.
Under the second contract, CRPO 170, Saipem will undertake EPCI work at the Marjan field, including three production deck manifolds, approximately 25 kilometers of pipelines with diameters of 12 to 16 inches, and around 17 kilometers of 15 kV cables, together with associated subsea facilities.
Across the two contracts, the scope encompasses seven production deck manifolds, approximately 39 kilometers of pipelines and 41 kilometers of power cables.

Arabian Drilling Secures SAR 1.5 Billion Contract to Run Two KJO Vessels

Posted on 22 November 2026, 11:31 GMT 22 November 2026, 12:53 GMT
Download on the App Store Get it on Google Play Follow us on Google Follow us on WhatsApp
The Arabian Drilling name in dark green letters beside an orange AD monogram, centred on a white background
Arabian Drilling, Saudi Arabia.

...

By The Edge Research Team
The Takeaway: Arabian Drilling’s SAR 1.5 billion Khafji contract is expected to add to its results from each vessel’s start date, the company said. Its release of 8 November, before the signing, reported record contracted work still to come of SAR 17.6 billion, and the filing does not say how the contract changes that figure. The filing gives no split of value between the vessels and no profit estimate.
ADVERTISEMENT Sponsorship Put your name on our market wraps, reports and results coverage Learn more →
Khafji Joint Operations (KJO) has contracted Arabian Drilling to provide and operate two self-propelled offshore service vessels in a SAR 1.5 billion deal, replacing existing contracted service for two vessels.
Arabian Drilling (2381) disclosed the contract to the Saudi Exchange on 22 November. It was published at 05:03 GMT. The filing dates both the award and the signing 19 November, three days earlier, and lists no related parties.

Two vessels, two terms

The contract covers the provision and operation of the two vessels for KJO. They are self-propelled, meaning they move under their own power, and the filing does not say what work they will do. The first is contracted for 10 years and the second for 15. The company expects the first to begin operating in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the second in the fourth quarter of 2028, and it expects the contract to contribute to its results from each start date.
Contract terms by vessel, as disclosed
* Vessel | Term | Expected start
* First | 10 years | Q4 2026
* Second | 15 years | Q4 2028
The filing gives the total value, SAR 1.5 billion, and no value for each vessel.
The filing does not say whether each term runs from the vessel’s start date, from signing or from another date, so end dates cannot be set from it.
Spread evenly over the 25 vessel-years in the two terms, the contract averages SAR 60 million per vessel-year.
That is $16 million at the riyal’s peg of 3.75 to the dollar. The Edge calculated these averages from the filed total. The filing prints no value for each vessel, and unequal rates would change them.
At equal rates, the two vessels would together average SAR 120 million a year once both are running, which the filing expects from the fourth quarter of 2028. The first vessel alone would average SAR 60 million. The release does not say which segment would report the vessels, and they replace existing contracted service, so the value is not all new revenue.

The contract replaces existing vessel service, and the filing’s two texts differ

The English text says the new contract “replaces two existing offshore service vessel contracts”. The Arabic text reads «يحل محل عقد منصتي خدمات بحرية قائمتين», which is one contract covering two existing platforms, and it uses «منصتي» for the new vessels too. The exchange page gives both texts the same date and time, so it does not show which came first.
The Arabic financial-impact line says the contract is expected to contribute to strengthening («تعزيز») the company’s results. Neither text names the counterparty of what is replaced, or gives its value or remaining terms. The filing therefore does not show how much of the contract is additional to what the vessels already earn.

The backlog the company has printed since September

...

It credits two gas awards on land and what it calls the KJO Dorra award covering four offshore rigs. The company’s filings do not use the name Dorra. The match with the 29 September award, on customer and rig count, is The Edge’s reading.
Arabian Drilling contract awards disclosed since 31 August 2026
* Disclosed | Scope | Term | Value as filed
* 31 Aug | SLB, 11 land rigs, gas | 5 years | About SAR 3 billion
* 14 Sep | SLB, 8 land rigs, gas | 5 years | About SAR 2 billion
* 29 Sep | KJO, 4 jack-up rigs | 4 years | About SAR 2 billion
* 22 Nov | KJO, 2 service vessels | 10 and 15 years | SAR 1.5 billion
Jack-up rigs are offshore drilling rigs that stand on the seabed. Values are the filings’ own; the first three are stated as approximate.
Two of these four are not new equipment. The 11 land rigs are the incumbent units under the company’s previous gas contract with SLB, and the 8 are redeployed from the existing fleet.

...

Land gross profit rose from SAR 80.5 million to SAR 96.7 million. The rise is SAR 16.2 million.
On 12 August the company said it had notice to resume its remaining suspended offshore rigs, and that it expected offshore fleet utilization to reach 100% by the end of the third quarter. The release gives no offshore utilization figure.

What the company says next

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise by approximately 8% to 10% on the third quarter, mainly from the start-up of the gas LSTK and KJO Dorra projects it was awarded. LSTK is the label the filings give the SLB gas work.
That range works out to SAR 876 million to SAR 892 million. The release predates the signing of the vessel contract and does not mention it.
It also raised its 2026 capital spending guidance to SAR 750 million to SAR 800 million, to ready rigs for contracted start dates. The earlier guidance was approximately SAR 700 million.

What the filing leaves out

The filing carries no revenue or profit estimate and no day rates. It does not describe the work the vessels do, name the counterparty of what is being replaced, give its value or end dates, or state any backlog figure.
What to watch: The filing expects the first vessel to begin operating in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the second in the fourth quarter of 2028.
Method: the contract’s value, counterparty, terms, start quarters and replacement are from Arabian Drilling’s announcement on the Saudi Exchange on 22 November 2026.
Backlog, results, segment, fleet, guidance and quotation figures are from the company’s nine-month results announcement and earnings release of 8 November 2026 and its announcements of 12 August, 31 August, 14 September and 29 September.
The per-vessel-year averages, the dollar equivalent at the riyal’s peg of SAR 3.75, the per-unit-year values and the fourth-quarter revenue range are The Edge’s calculations.
Sources: Saudi Exchange, Arabian Drilling, The Edge.

Arabian Drilling Secures $399.8M Offshore Vessel Contract With Khafji Joint Operations

Ola Noureldin

Arabian Drilling Secures $399.8M Offshore Vessel Contract With Khafji Joint Operations Founded in 1964, Arabian Drilling provides onshore and offshore oil and gas drilling services in Saudi Arabia. Image by Arabian Drilling
Saudi Arabia's Arabian Drilling has signed a $399.8 million (SAR 1.5 billion) long-term contract with Khafji Joint Operations (KJO) to provide and operate two self-propelled offshore vessels, raising its total order backlog to a record $4.9 billion ( SAR 18.5 billion) , the company announced Sunday.

Arabian Drilling-KJO contract details

* The agreement, which replaces existing contracts for two barges, covers operating periods of 10 and 15 years, marking the longest vessel contract secured by the Tadawul-listed drilling contractor to date.
* Under the agreement, the first vessel will operate for 10 years, with operations expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026. The second vessel will operate under a 15-year contract, with operations scheduled to commence in the fourth quarter of 2028.
* Arabian Drilling said the contract would begin contributing to its financial results as each vessel enters service, providing long-term revenue visibility.
* The agreement also allows the company to maintain its 100% market share with KJO in this service segment.
* In September, Arabian Drilling signed a four-year , $532.5 million (SAR 2 billion) contract with KJO to provide four high-specification offshore jack-up drilling rigs for KJO's offshore drilling operations.

Crucial quote

Fahad Albani, CEO of Arabian Drilling , said the agreement strengthens the company's longstanding relationship with KJO and reflects continued confidence in its operational capabilities. "This long-term contract marks an important milestone for Arabian Drilling and further strengthens our long-standing relationship with KJO," Albani said. He added that the company remains focused on executing its contracts, strengthening customer partnerships, and generating long-term shareholder value.

Key background

Founded in 1964, Arabian Drilling provides onshore and offshore oil and gas drilling services in Saudi Arabia. Its major shareholders include Industrialization & Energy Services Company (TAQA) and global energy technology company SLB.
The company, listed on the Saudi Exchange, serves clients including Saudi Aramco and KJO and operates a fleet of onshore and offshore drilling rigs.
The latest agreement expands Arabian Drilling's contracted revenue base, with the two vessels expected to contribute to earnings over the next decade and beyond.

Arabian Drilling financial performance

Arabian Drilling posted a net profit of $8.4 million in the third quarter of 2026 , reversing a loss of the same amount in the previous quarter, as offshore drilling operations resumed and cost-efficiency measures supported earnings, according to a bourse filing.
The Saudi-listed company reported third-quarter revenue of $216.2 million (SAR 810.7 million), up 6% from $203.9 million (SAR 764.7 million) in the previous quarter, the filing released on the Saudi Exchange showed Sunday. However, revenue declined 2.9% from $222.8 million (SAR 835.4 million) a year earlier, primarily due to lower rig activity.
Despite the quarterly rebound, Arabian Drilling's revenue for the first nine months of 2026 fell 8.1% year-on-year to $639.2 million (SAR 2.397 billion), from $695.7 million (SAR 2.609 billion), due to temporary suspensions of offshore drilling operations and the absence of extended rig-move activities.

Big number

Arabian Drilling expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise by approximately 8% to 10% from the third quarter, supported by higher drilling activity. The company also raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to between $200 million and $213 million (SAR 750 million–SAR 800 million) to accelerate rig preparations and deployment under recently awarded contracts.
